title: As a backend developer, I write workflows as ordinary code in my language — steps with automatic checkpointing — not YAML or a proprietary DSL
As a backend developer, I author workflows in the language my team already uses — TypeScript, Python, Go, or more — with real feature parity across SDKs
As a backend developer, I compose workflows from parallel steps, fan-out/fan-in over dynamic batches, and child workflows without hand-rolling coordination
As a backend developer, every step retries automatically with configurable backoff, timeouts, and failure policies — no try/catch scaffolding
As a backend developer, a workflow interrupted by a process crash, deploy, or infrastructure failure resumes from its last completed step with state intact
As a backend developer, a workflow can sleep or wait for days to months without holding a server, connection, or billable compute
As a backend developer, idempotency keys and exactly-once step semantics stop duplicate triggers from double-charging or double-sending
As a backend developer, I schedule workflows on cron expressions with overlap policies, pause/resume, and visibility into upcoming runs
As a backend developer, events from my app, webhooks, or queues trigger workflows declaratively, and one event can fan out to many functions
As a backend developer, I debounce, batch, or delay triggers so noisy event streams collapse into the runs I actually want
As a backend developer, a workflow pauses for human approval or input for hours or days and resumes the moment the response arrives
As a backend developer, I send signals, events, or messages into a specific running workflow from outside — an API call, webhook, or another workflow
As a platform engineer, every run has a step-by-step timeline — inputs, outputs, retries, and errors per step — in a dashboard my team can search and filter
As a platform engineer, I replay or rerun a failed workflow from its recorded history — optionally from a specific step — to debug and recover
As a platform engineer, failure rates, latencies, and queue depths export to my observability stack, and alerts fire when workflows misbehave
As a platform engineer, I deploy new workflow code while in-flight runs finish on the version they started with — versioning without breaking determinism
As a platform engineer, throughput scales by adding workers — the platform load-balances tasks across the fleet and tolerates worker loss
As a platform engineer, I cap concurrency and set rate limits per workflow, per key, or per tenant so one hot customer can't starve the rest
As a platform engineer, I assign priorities to runs and get fair scheduling across tenants instead of a single FIFO queue
As an agent builder, I run LLM agent loops as durable workflows — model and tool calls as checkpointed, retried steps that survive crashes mid-run
As an agent builder, first-party integrations wrap my AI stack — AI SDKs, agent frameworks, model providers — so agent steps get durability without glue code
As an AI-native user, I stream live progress — step updates or model tokens — from a running workflow into my frontend as it executes
As a backend developer, one command runs the whole engine locally, and testing utilities let me unit-test workflows with time skipping and mocked steps
As a platform engineer, I run workers in my own infrastructure while the vendor manages the orchestration control plane — code and data stay inside my network
